blocks.text: Teacher Graphic Organizer Toolkit
U.S. History Hack™ · Unit 1 — The Rise of Industrialization (1877–1900) · US.01–US.07. Reproducible — you may copy these pages for classroom use.

blocks.label: Why this toolkit
paras: Knowing WHICH organizer to use, and WHEN, is half the battle. This toolkit tells you — with a brief why for each — then gives you reproducible blanks (Part 1) and per-standard Cornell support backs (Part 2). Tennessee connections are highlighted throughout; the local-to-national move is a History Hack signature and a point of difference for our classrooms.

blocks.text: Part 1 — Reusable Blank Organizers
Content-agnostic blanks. Print as many as you need; use across any standard or subject.
Venn Diagram (2)
Task says “compare,” “contrast,” “how are they alike/different?” for TWO things.
blocks.cite: Marzano's #1 strategy (identifying similarities & differences); the shared zone forces students to name what overlaps.

blocks.text: Venn (3) / Triple Compare
Comparing three people, groups, or ideas across the same traits.
blocks.cite: Extends comparison to three items without losing structure.

blocks.text: T-Chart
Two categories to sort or weigh: benefits vs costs, pros vs cons, before vs after, cause vs effect.
blocks.cite: Fast, low-floor entry point for comparison.

blocks.text: Compare & Contrast Matrix
Comparing several items across the SAME set of criteria.
blocks.cite: Reduces cognitive load by making the comparison systematic.

blocks.text: Cause & Effect
Task asks “what caused…?”, “what were the effects/consequences of…?”
Timeline / Sequence
Ordering events or tracing change over time.
Concept Web
Activating prior knowledge or showing how ideas relate to a central concept.
blocks.cite: Great as a pre-reading or review move.

blocks.text: Main Idea & Details
Pulling the central idea and its support from a text or source.
blocks.cite: Separates the big idea from the evidence.

blocks.text: KWL
Start of a standard: what students Know / Want to know; end: what they Learned.

head: K — what I Know
W — what I Want to know
L — what I Learned

blocks.text: 5 Ws
blocks.tag: Cover the Basics of an Event

blocks.text: Making sure students capture who/what/when/where/why of an event before analysis.
Problem & Solution
Analyzing a problem and the responses to it (e.g., a policy or reform).
Frayer Model
Learning a key term deeply (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples).

blocks.extend: push higher-DOK — “Give a non-example that is easy to confuse with this term, and explain the difference.”

blocks.text: CER
Any “make a claim / defend / argue” task. Claim + two pieces of evidence + reasoning.
HIPPO
Analyzing a photo, cartoon, map, or document. Pair with OPTIC for visuals.
Tennessee Connection
Whenever a standard has a Tennessee tie: link the national event to our state/community and say why the local story matters.
blocks.cite: The local-to-national move — a History Hack signature.

US.01 — Homestead Act and Transcontinental Railroad
Reproducible — scaffolds ONLY the Cornell notes for this standard. Copy for students who need them; fade as evidence grows. Not a track, not a separate grade.
Guided Support

head: Key vocabulary
What it means
rows: An 1862 law that provided 160 acres of public land to settlers who agreed to live on and improve the land for five years, encouraging westward expansion.
A continuous railroad line completed in 1869 that connected the eastern United States with the Pacific coast, revolutionizing transportation and commerce.
The 19th-century movement of settlers, railroads, and U.S. authority across the continent toward the Pacific, encouraged by free land and new transportation.

blocks.text: US.05 — Inventions & Innovations of Business Leaders & Entrepreneurs
Reproducible — scaffolds ONLY the Cornell notes for this standard. Copy for students who need them; fade as evidence grows. Not a track, not a separate grade.
Guided Support

head: Key vocabulary
What it means
rows: Wealthy industrialists of the late 1800s who built massive business empires. Critics called them "robber barons" for ruthless practices; supporters called them "captains of industry" for economic growth.
A business strategy where a company controls all stages of production, from raw materials to finished product, as practiced by Andrew Carnegie in the steel industry.
A business strategy where a company buys out competitors in the same industry to reduce competition and control prices, as practiced by John D. Rockefeller in oil.

What it means
